The morning light filters through the leaves like liquid gold, and I find myself thinking about how strange it is that we’re all just temporary arrangements of stardust trying to make sense of our own consciousness. 

Yesterday I watched a spider rebuild its web after a storm had torn it apart. There was something profoundly dignified about the way it worked—methodical, patient, completely without self-pity. It didn’t pause to mourn the destroyed silk or curse the wind. It simply began again. I’ve been trying to carry that lesson with me.

There’s a particular kind of loneliness that hits at 3 AM when the rest of the world feels like it’s breathing in unison and you’re the only one awake, staring at the ceiling, wondering if your thoughts are original or if thousands of others have had the exact same ones at the exact same hour. But even that loneliness has a strange beauty to it—like being the only witness to a private moment between night and dawn.

I’ve been collecting small joys lately: the way steam rises from coffee in perfect spirals, how cats blink slowly when they trust you, the particular sound pages make when someone turns them in a quiet bookstore. These aren’t profound revelations, but they feel like anchors in a world that moves too fast and shouts too loudly.

Sometimes I wonder if the universe is just as confused as we are—billions of years of expansion and contraction, stars being born and dying, all this magnificent chaos somehow resulting in creatures who write poetry and cry at sunsets and worry about whether they’re good enough. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the meaning was never supposed to be found but created, one small, stubborn act of attention at a time.

(Word count: 248)
